source: Qin, Xia, Wang et al. (2024) Relevant or Random: Can LLMs Truly Perform Analogical Reasoning?
finding: Re-tested Yasunaga's self-generated-exemplar method with irrelevant self-generated examples as controls. On math, irrelevant examples beat relevant ones. On BBH, relevant ones won slightly. The accuracy of the self-made examples, not their relevance, tracked the gain.
numbers: GPT-3.5-turbo, 500 test items per dataset, 3 seeds. GSM8K: relevant 71.5, N/A-topic 75.5, random-same 75.1, random-different 76.3, random-biology 75.3. MATH: relevant 33.3, N/A 36.1. BBH 5-task mean: relevant 63.2, N/A 61.9, random-same 60.4, random-diff 56.4, random-bio 61.7. Example accuracy on MATH: relevant 62%, N/A 72%, random-same 86%. Llama-2-70B GSM8K: relevant 45.1 vs random-diff 54.3. Llama-3-8B: 69.5 vs 74.1. Fixed hand-checked ICL examples (math or biology) reached 75.8-76.8 on Llama-3-8B and beat all self-generated variants.
quote: self-generated random examples can surprisingly achieve comparable or even better performance
limits: Only GPT-3.5-turbo and Llama models; no frontier model. Relevant-recall prompt is one 5-example template. The relevant arm is below plain N/A on GSM8K here, which differs from Yasunaga's small gain.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'recall similar problems' helps a strong model. Treat the step as a test arm; check example correctness, and prefer a verified fixed bank over self-recalled analogues for math.

source: Chan, Fu, Schunn, Cagan, Wood, Kotovsky (2011) On the Benefits and Pitfalls of Analogies for Innovative Design: Ideation Performance Based on Analogical Distance, Commonness, and Modality of Examples
finding: Full text re-opened. Confirms the K08 and K09 numbers. Far-field examples raised solution transfer, variability of quality and mean novelty, but cut quantity. Less-common examples raised quantity, breadth and novelty. Only the far-field plus less-common cell beat the control on novelty.
numbers: Senior engineering students; 1,321 ideas coded, 1,066 kept after the constraint screen. Table 1 cell counts sum to 151 as parsed (K08 says N=153). Distance main effect on transfer eta2=0.08 (far more transfer than near, d=0.60); on quantity eta2=0.05 (far fewer than near, d=-0.30); variability of quality eta2=0.06 (far vs near d=0.64, far vs control d=0.78); mean novelty far vs near d=0.56. Commonness: quantity eta2=0.12 (more-common fewer than less-common d=-0.67, fewer than control d=-0.76); breadth more-common vs control d=-1.03, vs less-common d=-0.61; mean novelty less- vs more-common d=0.61. Dunnett: far+less-common vs control mean novelty d=1.14. Kappa 0.72 (feasibility screen), 0.84 (solution types).
limits: One design problem (energy from human motion), two examples per cell, patents as examples, students not experts, first ideation phase only. Mean and max quality were NOT changed by distance or commonness. Many ideas were not developed enough to judge feasibility.
agent_relevance: Far and uncommon sources raise novelty but not quality and cost quantity. Pair a far source with a feasibility filter. Check source commonness, not only distance.

source: Ye, Wang, Choi et al. (2024) AnaloBench: Benchmarking the Identification of Abstract and Long-context Analogies (EMNLP 2024, arXiv v2 HTML)
finding: Re-read the T1 table. The Introduction says the human-GPT-4 gap is 6.9 points at 1 sentence and 28.8 at 30 sentences. The paper's own Table 2 and Table 7 give 6.9 and 12.6. The 28.8 figure is an internal error. Claude-v2 is near random at 10 and 30 sentences.
numbers: T1 analogy selection (4 options, chance 25%), 1/10/30 sentences: GPT-4 89.1/66.5/60.7; Claude-v2 68.2/30.2/25.9; GPT-3.5 65.3/46.4/30.8; human 96.0/72.5/73.3. Gaps: 96.0-89.1=6.9; 72.5-66.5=6.0; 73.3-60.7=12.6. Table 3 (10/30 sentences): Claude on Claude stories 36.5/33.5; GPT-4 on Claude stories 69.7/57.6; GPT-4 on its own 66.5/60.7.
quote: the gap between humans and GPT4 is 6.9% on 1-sentence stories, but increases to 28.8% on 30-sentence stories
limits: Models are 2023 models. Human numbers come from a small annotated sample. Story elaboration was done by GPT-4, with a Claude-v2 check.
agent_relevance: Fixes the K14 number. Long, noisy source text hurts retrieval, so compress before matching.

source: Ye, Wang, Choi et al. (2024) AnaloBench, T2 story-bank retrieval, Appendix G (Table 8)
finding: T2 asks for the top 10 analogous stories from a bank of 200. GPT-4-Turbo is clearly above the random baseline only for 1-sentence stories. At 10 and 30 sentences it is close to the random list. Claude-v2 is near random everywhere. No newer model has been run on this table in the papers I found.
numbers: GPT-4-Turbo, 1/10/30 sentences: P@3 42.9/6.5/3.9; P@5 38.5/5.2/3.6; R@3 20.1/2.9/1.8; R@5 29.7/3.8/2.7; MAP 55.4/14.2/10.8; MRR 64.2/15.6/11.3. Claude-v2 P@3 10.2/5.3/5.4; MAP 6.3/1.9/3.4. Random P@3 3.9; oracle recall@3 48.9%. The random baseline is the list 1..10 because models default to that list on hard prompts.
quote: Both models perform similarly to the trivial baseline in most cases
limits: No 2025-2026 frontier model was evaluated. The HTML table header is flattened; the column mapping (GPT-4-Turbo first three, Claude-v2 next three, then random, oracle) was inferred from the 8-value rows and matches the text.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 stays open: a clean rerun with current models must be done by us. Do not rely on a model's unaided recall from a large bank; use an embedding or reranker stage.

source: Ye et al. (2024) AnaloBench, Table 4 (accuracy on true-positive human predictions)
finding: On the low-error item set (items humans got right), the same trend holds, and GPT-4 falls much harder with length than the headline table shows.
limits: Subset size not checked; its 30-sentence GPT-4 number (22.7) is below chance for a 4-way task and conflicts with the full-set 60.7. Do not cite without checking the subset.
agent_relevance: Warns that the 30-sentence GPT-4 number is unstable and depends on the item set.

source: Yasunaga, Chen, Yu et al. (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners (ICLR 2024; tables re-decoded from PDF text)
finding: Re-read Tables 1 and 2. Row labels are lost in the PDF text but row counts match the method list. The baseline ambiguity is resolved: 14.8% for text-davinci-003 is the plain 0-shot row and 5-shot CoT is 54.0%, so the gain over the best baseline is 7 points, not 46.
numbers: GSM8K (decoded): GPT-3.5-turbo 0-shot 75.0, 0-shot CoT 75.8, 5-shot CoT 76.7, self-generated 77.8 (+1.1 over best baseline). text-davinci-003: 14.8, 50.3, 54.0, 61.0. PaLM2: 60.8, 78.2, 80.7, 81.7. MATH GPT-3.5: 33.0, 33.9, 34.9, 37.3; PaLM2 27.1, 29.8, 34.3, 34.8. Codeforces Acc@1 (5 rows: 0-shot, 0-shot CoT, 3-shot CoT, exemplars, knowledge+exemplars): GPT-3.5-16k 8, 9, 11, 13, 15; GPT-4 16, 16, 17, 17, 19. Acc@10 GPT-4 30, 29, 31, 32, 37.
limits: Row assignment inferred from the layout; the paper's own table is the final word. GPT-4 was not run on GSM8K or MATH. Single run, no variance reported.
agent_relevance: On a strong model the headline gain is small (about 1 point on GSM8K, 3 on Codeforces Acc@1). Run it as an A/B arm, never as a default.

source: Gwak, Jung, Park et al. (2026) Not the Example, but the Process: How Self-Generated Examples Enhance LLM Reasoning
finding: Tests recent chat models, not only weak ones. Making the model write a related problem inside the same prompt helps (Integrated). Reusing those examples in a fresh prompt (Decoupled) gives almost nothing. Gains shrink once chain-of-thought is on.
numbers: No-CoT, full GSM8K (1,319) and MATH. GSM8K zero-shot / integrated / decoupled: GPT-4.1 48.8 / 57.9 / 49.1; GPT-4o 49.9 / 54.6 / 50.5; Gemini-1.5-Flash 36.0 / 41.2 / 36.5; Llama-3.3-70B 32.7 / 35.2 / 33.6; Llama-3.1-8B 12.1 / 16.5 / 11.6. MATH: GPT-4.1 33.3 / 39.4 / 37.4; GPT-4o 33.3 / 37.9 / 32.6. Reusing integrated examples in decoupled form (GPT-4o): GSM8K 52.2, MATH 33.7. With CoT on MATH: GPT-4o-mini 75.36 / 76.59 / 72.90; Gemini 78.23 / 79.06 / 78.65. Stating the intention: GSM8K decoupled 33.59 to 41.60; integrated 35.19 to 45.50.
limits: The no-CoT zero-shot baselines are far below published GSM8K scores for these models, so the +5 to +9 gains partly reflect forced extra reasoning text. Models are 2024-era chat models, not reasoning models. The relevance question is not tested here.
agent_relevance: The gain looks like a thinking-aloud effect, not an analogy-retrieval effect. With CoT the gain is about 1 point. Do not credit analogy for it.

source: Jung, Kim, Kim et al. (2026) Cross-Pollination Retrieval: Finding Transferable Ideas Across Fields in Scientific Literature
finding: Re-opened for the representation and cost questions (gap 2). On one shared pool of 151 candidates per query, an LLM tournament reranker beats every embedding model and every query-rewriting trick. The query is a domain-stripped 'How to ...' problem. The 0.81 holds only when the correct paper is already in the pool.
numbers: CPR-eval: 1,300 queries, 26 fields, 151 candidates per query (50 are same-topic distractors). Best of 11 retrievers Recall@10 0.26 (Gemini Embedding, inf-retriever-v1-pro), random 0.07, SPECTER2 0.09. LLM reranker (MiMo-V2.6-Pro, tournament, 151 to 10 in two rounds, then score the 10 singly) Recall@10 0.81. Fine-tuning on 10,573 pairs: Qwen3-0.6B 0.12 to 0.50, Qwen3-4B 0.17 to 0.69, Nemotron-8B 0.25 to 0.70. HyDE+BM25 0.16 to 0.44. After removing same-topic candidates retrievers reach at most 3.6x random, reranker 8.5x. On AnaloBench, training on CPR-train raises nDCG@10 by 0.04 to 0.12; MS MARCO, ReasonIR and SPECTER data lower it; without hard negatives most of the AnaloBench gain vanishes.
limits: Pool-based, not full corpus. Queries were written by an LLM from the citing paper. Reranker cost is not reported in tokens. No function-skeleton vs purpose-only vs full-text arm.
agent_relevance: Best current evidence that a cheap first stage plus an LLM rerank is the right shape. Query rewriting (HyDE) is a weak substitute for a rerank. Gap 2 is only partly closed.

source: Sharon and Hope (2026) RATIO: A Benchmark for Retrieval Across Typed Ideation Operations in Scientific Literature
finding: Benchmark of three retrieval moves (ADDRESS a problem, BROADEN to a general form, SPECIFY an instance). Fine-tuning helps each retriever most on its own move, and a GPT-5-mini listwise rerank of the top 100 adds more. First-stage recall caps the rerank.
numbers: Test pool 404,371 sentences. Rerank adds 8.4 to 15.5 MRR@10 points on SPECIFY and ADDRESS. ModernBERT-embed-large: tuning plus rerank adds 28.4 (SPECIFY) and 27.5 (ADDRESS) over baseline, tuning alone at most 20.0, rerank alone at most 14.3. Gold sentence in the tuned top 100 for 80.8% SPECIFY, 61.3% ADDRESS, 57.2% BROADEN; given that, the reranker puts it in the top 10 in 86.6%, 85.1%, 71.6%. Blind human check: 5 CS graduate students labelled 125 queries; a useful non-gold candidate appeared in the tuned top 10 for 64.8% of queries.
limits: CS papers and sentences, not engineering artefacts or biology. Gold is the next sentence in the source paper, so it is a proxy. Annotators were graduate students, N=5.
agent_relevance: Supports splitting the agent's retrieval into typed moves (abstract up, specify down, address) and reranking from a wide first stage.

source: Chen, Chen, Sun, Zhang (2026) Analogical Deep Research: Retrieving and Integrating Historical Analogies for Foresight Analysis
finding: Commercial deep-research agents with frontier backbones mostly fail to find structural analogies because they match surface features. A structural-decomposition step before retrieval helps. A cheap summarise-then-generate step recovers much of the gain for strong models.
numbers: ADR-bench: 15 events (10 historical with documented analogies, 5 forward). Four agents (OpenAI, Gemini, Qwen Deep Research, MiroFlow) with Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.4, Qwen3-8B backbones. Table 1 MDS score (GPT-5.4 judge): Sonnet-4.6 direct 2.24, summarise 3.91, self-reflection 4.11, CANA 4.17. GPT-5.4-mini direct 3.05, summarise 3.59, self-reflection 3.34, CANA 4.01. Qwen3-8B direct 1.76, summarise 3.47, self-reflection 3.94. MDS saturates near 4.1-4.2 for Sonnet-4.6. Claimed up to 25% over self-reflection on their 9-item rubric with GPT-5.4-mini.
limits: Only 15 events; LLM judge; the authors' own method and rubric; no equal-token control (CANA uses several rounds); no best-of-N arm. Foresight task, not design.
agent_relevance: For a strong model the structural-decomposition step adds little over a plain summary step (4.17 vs 3.91). Gap 1 stays open.

source: Shen, de Sousa, Barcelos, Guo, Zhu (2026) On the Diversity of Analogy Making in Large Language Models
finding: Ten recent LLMs asked to write analogies show domain homogeneity: they keep landing on the same few target domains, even when told to be diverse. Diversity tricks (top-k, top-p, entropy steering) raise diversity but cost quality. This is the LLM version of source-locking.
numbers: Best closed model on the diverse prompt (Gemini 3.1 Pro): intra-output diversity only 0.49; on extracted target domains diversity never above 0.63. Mistral-7B base prompt: quality 4.32, diversity 0.33, 1.97 target-domain clusters; Top-k: quality 4.21, diversity 0.53, 2.27 clusters. Same method ranks differently across models: Top-p and G2 reach 0.61 on Llama-3.1-8B but 0.28 and 0.29 on Qwen-3-8B. Quality judged by GPT-4o-mini. Data-pollution check: highest exact-match recovery 14%.
limits: Quality is an LLM-judge score on a 1-5 scale; prompts are single-sentence sources, not engineering problems. The steering part uses 7-9B open models.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that without a forcing step an LLM re-uses the same few source domains. Use a 'source already used' ledger and force a different domain.

source: Shen, Druckmann, Zou (2026) Unlocking LLM Creativity in Science through Analogical Reasoning
finding: Closest test yet of gaps 1 and 4. Explicit analogy generation (find a cross-domain problem with the same relational structure, then borrow its solution) beats a 'search other domains' prompt and a plain prompt on diversity and novelty, at the same number of calls as the cross-domain arm. The baselines mode-collapse.
numbers: Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3 Flash, temperature 1.0, biomedical research problems, 150 generations per problem. Calls per generation: AR 2, cross-domain 2, no-domain 1. Baseline domain Vendi 2.64 and 2.84; solution Vendi 5.81 and 8.34; only about 5% of domains (7-8 unique) and 57-66% of solutions unique. AR raises diversity metrics by 90-173%. Binary novelty (no-domain < cross-domain < AR): Claude 1.6% < 21.6% < 50.4%; GPT 9.0% < 28.2% < 58.8%; Gemini 8.9% < 37.8% < 68.9%. Stratified novelty Claude 1.28 < 3.12 < 5.54. Human pairwise: AR judged more novel 78% (kappa 0.445) and reasonable 67%. Cost about $0.02 per problem. Four AR solutions implemented with a coding agent.
limits: Novelty and diversity are LLM-judged (human-validated). No correctness or feasibility measure beyond 4 implemented cases. No best-of-N arm and tokens per call not matched. Biomedicine only.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit analogy step as a diversity and novelty engine, not as an accuracy booster. Gap 1 only half closed, since the control is another prompt, not resampling.

source: Zhu, Zhang, Luo (2022) Biologically Inspired Design Concept Generation Using Generative Pre-Trained Transformers, Section 5.3 re-read
finding: The only human feasibility check in this paper is tiny. Two concepts per generator type (about 6 generated concepts) plus 2 AskNature controls were rated by a 10-person flying-car team; 9 returned usable answers. The paper gives no failure reasons for infeasible concepts beyond infeasible numbers.
numbers: Raters: 10 engineers returned, 9 usable. Concepts rated: 2 each from Type-1, Type-2, Type-3 generators plus 2 AskNature controls. Type-1 and Type-2: lower feasibility, higher novelty than controls; Type-3: more feasible, less novel. Listed limits: GPT-3 cost, explorative output, infeasible numbers.
limits: Concepts passed a relevancy filter first, so not a random sample. One case. No pass or fail counts.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open: no pass rate exists. We must run our own blind check with failure categories.

source: Kang, Lin, Chen, Hong, Martelaro, Kittur (2025) BioSpark: Beyond Analogical Inspiration to LLM-augmented Transfer (CHI 2025)
finding: Within-subject study. An LLM-assisted bio-inspired design tool (mechanism clusters from a tree of life, 'sparks' from GPT-4-turbo) roughly doubled ideas and species used and raised blind-judged novelty and value, but feasibility scores went down.
numbers: 12 participants, within-subject vs AskNature baseline. Novelty 3.9 (SD 1.67) to 7.1 (1.03); value 3.8 (1.68) to 7.0 (0.91); feasibility 6.8 (1.37) to 5.7 (1.02). Overall quality 4.48 to 6.52 (mixed model, p<0.0001). Ideas per person 5.5 to 10.3 (paired p=0.04). Unique species 4.6 to 8.2 (p=0.007). Expert ICC: novelty 0.94, feasibility 0.74, value 0.90.
limits: N=12 researchers, not engineers; 1-10 rubric; two judges; tool use, not an agent. A significance test for the feasibility drop was not seen in the text read.
agent_relevance: Feasibility falls when novelty rises; add a feasibility critic. More species used is the human analogue of a forced second source.

source: Chen, Song, Zheng, Jing, Hansen, Sun (2025) Understanding Design Fixation in Generative AI
finding: First report that a GenAI text model also repeats itself in design. Small study: ChatGPT chair designs used a less varied vocabulary than award-winning human designs, and most designers noticed the repetition. It does not test bio-inspired design or a mitigation step.
numbers: 10 participants, 30-minute sessions, ChatGPT (GPT-4o) and Midjourney. Share of unique terms: ChatGPT 67.4% vs Red Dot human entries 78.2%. 7 of 10 noticed repetition in ChatGPT, 8 of 10 in Midjourney.
limits: N=10 novice designers; word-frequency measure; one product type; no source tracking; no forced-second-source arm.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open: no study counts same-source repeats in bio-inspired design with and without a forced second source.

source: Fu, Chan, Cagan, Kotovsky, Schunn, Wood (2013) The Meaning of Near and Far (JMD 135(2)) - attempted
finding: Full text NOT obtained. The Pitt URL returns an HTML error page; Springer and NSF mirrors were blocked or empty. What I know comes from secondary snippets: it used the U.S. patent database, argued near and far are relative, and suggested a curvilinear (sweet spot) relation.
numbers: No N, effect sizes or peak distance recovered.
limits: Secondary claims only; the later-paper description of a sweet spot is not checked against the primary paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open for Fu 2013, Linsey 2012 and Christensen and Schunn 2007. Do not cite a sweet-spot distance.

source: Examining the boundary between near and far design stimuli (Design Society proceedings, abstract page only)
finding: Abstract page only. Participants rated similarity of 3D-part triplets and sorted them; computed distances showed distinct boundaries beyond which stimuli were too far, and those boundaries fell at larger distances for visual than for functional similarity.
numbers: N=36 participants. No effect sizes on the page.
limits: Abstract only; authors and year not confirmed; no design-outcome measure.
agent_relevance: Where too far begins depends on whether similarity is visual or functional, so measure distance on function, not appearance.
